items.title: The Glorious Revolution was a Dutch invasion
items.claim: William of Orange landed in Devon on 5 November 1688. How large was the force?

options.text: A diplomatic mission of a few hundred men
Around 15,000 troops on 463 ships — larger than the Spanish Armada
Only James II's English defectors, no foreign troops
A small English army recruited in advance by Parliament

items.reveal:
Seven English nobles (the 'Immortal Seven') invited William in June 1688. He landed at Brixham, Devon, with 15,000-21,000 Dutch troops, plus thousands of horses and 50 cannon. James II's army melted; key officers (including John Churchill, the future Duke of Marlborough) defected.

James fled to France in December. The Convention Parliament (January 1689) declared the throne vacant and offered it to William and Mary. The Bill of Rights followed in December 1689.

The Williamite War in Ireland (Boyne 1690) and the Highland war in Scotland (Killiecrankie 1689) were anything but bloodless.
items.why: The 'Glorious Revolution' as bloodless English self-determination is a Whig myth. It was a foreign-backed coup with extensive bloodshed in Ireland and Scotland — successful, but not peaceful.

items.title: The Luddites were skilled workers protecting trade standards

options.text: Anti-technology mystics who rejected all machinery
Skilled textile workers — stocking knitters, croppers, weavers — who smashed specific machines being used to produce low-quality goods by unapprenticed labour, often after pay cuts and food shortages

items.reveal:
The Luddites took their name from the mythical Ned Ludd. Their grievances were specific: wide stocking frames produced cut-up goods sold as stockings; gig-mills and shearing frames replaced cropping; manufacturers were ignoring the Statute of Artificers (1563) requiring seven-year apprenticeships.

The Frame-Breaking Act (1812) made machine-breaking a capital offence — Byron made his maiden speech in the Lords opposing it. 17 Luddites were hanged at York in January 1813. The historian E. P. Thompson's 'The Making of the English Working Class' (1963) rehabilitated them as political actors.
items.why: 'Luddite' as an insult against anyone who dislikes new technology obscures the actual movement. They were skilled tradesmen defending wages and standards against unregulated mechanisation — not opponents of machinery in principle.

items.title: Cholera transmission was solved by removing a pump handle
items.claim: In the 1854 Soho outbreak, what did John Snow do?

options.text: He developed the first cholera vaccine
He mapped deaths around Broad Street, identified the public water pump as the source, and persuaded authorities to remove its handle on 8 September 1854

items.reveal:
Snow's spot map of Broad Street showed deaths clustered around one pump. He overruled the dominant 'miasma' (bad air) theory of disease.

The pump handle was removed and cases fell. The cause was a leaking cesspit contaminating the well. Snow published 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' in 1855 — but his germ theory was not widely accepted until the 1860s with Pasteur and Koch.

London's main response was Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system (1859-1875), built largely after the 'Great Stink' of 1858 made Parliament unbearable.
items.why: Public health is often credited to grand theories. The 1854 case shows that careful observation and a map could outperform the dominant medical theory of the day — even before the underlying biology was understood.
